summary: Teaches 5-7 year olds simple garden food chains: who eats whom (leaf → caterpillar → bird), that minibeasts are both eaters and eaten, and that the arrow means 'is eaten by' / energy flows toward the eater. Core activity is constructing a short chain and reading the arrows aloud; a quiz and a tap-to-reveal scene are companions; role-play is an alternative for surfacing the middle-of-chain idea. The eater is identified by its role in the chain, not by being the bigger animal.
misconceptions: Arrow-direction reversal — children read 'bird → caterpillar' as 'the bird is eaten by the caterpillar'; the arrow points to the eater.
'A creature is either a hunter or food' — not grasping that a minibeast can be both (eats plants, eaten by birds).
'Chains start with an animal' — missing that the plant is the starting food source.
'Big animals always eat small ones / the last animal is the strongest' — size and 'winner' confusions.
Treating the chain as who-is-friends-with-whom rather than who-eats-whom.

activities.title: Build and read a garden food chain
steps: Start with a shuffled set of garden organism cards — leaf, caterpillar, blue tit — and arrange them into the correct order to show who eats what.
Place the caterpillar next to the leaf and draw or confirm an arrow from leaf to caterpillar (leaf → caterpillar).
Add the bird after the caterpillar and draw the arrow caterpillar → bird.
Tap or point to the caterpillar in the middle and say both things about it: 'I eat the leaf' AND 'the bird eats me'.
Read the finished chain aloud using the arrow convention: 'the leaf is eaten by the caterpillar, the caterpillar is eaten by the bird'.

Try the deliberate wrong move of linking the leaf directly to the blue tit (leaf → blue tit, skipping the caterpillar) to see why it does not fit this chain: in this chain the caterpillar eats the leaf and the blue tit eats the caterpillar.
Optionally remove one link and say what happens to the chain.
activities.insight: The arrow points from the food to the eater (it means 'is eaten by' and shows energy passing along), and a minibeast in the middle is both an eater and something that is eaten.

activities.title: Order, match and choose the arrow direction (companion checks)
steps: Put the three organism cards (leaf, caterpillar, bird) in the correct sequence.
Match each eater to its food (bird ↔ caterpillar, caterpillar ↔ leaf).
Choose which way the arrow points between the caterpillar and the bird, and say what it means.
activities.insight: Who-eats-whom order and arrow direction can be stated reliably and transferred to a new chain.

activities.title: Interview a caterpillar (role-play alternative)
steps: Pretend to be a caterpillar and answer two questions aloud: 'What do I eat?' and 'Who eats me?'
Say the sentence 'I eat the leaf and the bird eats me' to capture the middle-of-chain idea.
Swap roles and interview a ladybird to find out it hunts aphids.
activities.insight: A minibeast sits in the middle of a chain — it both eats and is eaten — and even a tiny creature can be a hunter.

activities.title: Read the arrow in a labelled garden scene (scaffold)
steps: Look at a garden picture with a pre-drawn chain leaf → caterpillar → bird.
Tap or lift the 'what does the arrow mean?' label and read the explanation aloud.
Point along the chain in the direction the energy travels.
activities.insight: The arrow between two organisms means 'is eaten by' and shows energy moving to the eater.

checkQuestion: In the food chain leaf → caterpillar → bird, what does the arrow between the caterpillar and the bird mean — who eats whom? And does the caterpillar eat anything itself?
checkAnswer: The arrow points from the caterpillar TO the bird, meaning the caterpillar is eaten BY the bird (the food and energy pass to the bird). And yes — the caterpillar itself eats leaves. Minibeasts both eat (plants or smaller creatures) and are eaten by bigger animals.
